narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Compare two source-specific roles: Plutarch’s Theseus brings Attica into a civic community, while the Library’s Heracles serves Eurystheus through imposed labours. These are useful contrasts, not exhaustive definitions of either hero.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “together all the inhabitants of Attica into one town, and made them one people of one city, whereas before they lived dispersed, and were not easy to assemble upon any affair for the common interest. Nay, differences and even wars often occurred between them, which he by his persuasions appeased, going”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: Different communities need different heroes. The comparison reveals what each tradition is trying to justify or preserve.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Keep both citations in view. Plutarch supports the civic-founder comparison; the Library supports imposed service. Neither passage defines everything that Theseus or Heracles can mean in other works.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Civic heroism turns power into an account of belonging and order.
